name: Biganjutsu facial care

card.summary: An early-twentieth-century Japanese facial regimen of hot towels, cream massage and electrotherapy that treated skin care as hygiene, aiming for smooth, clear skin with a natural-looking complexion.
card.aka: Japanese hygienic facial care, hygienic facial culture
card.note: A historical practice; modern equivalents vary by salon and device.

quick.overview:
Biganjutsu, roughly "the technique of the beautiful face," was a Japanese approach that made facial skin care a matter of hygiene rather than makeup alone. A typical urban facial used a hot towel to open the pores, massage with cream and electrotherapeutic devices.

The goal was smooth skin free of blemishes and wrinkles and a healthy complexion with a natural look, with less reliance on heavy cosmetics. Historians describe it as a precursor to Japan's modern aesthetics (esute) industry; no clinical research evaluates the original regimen.
quick.how: Historical accounts describe salon facials: warm towel, massage with cream, and electrically driven treatment. The term later broadened to cover other beauty services.
quick.risks: No documented risks are reported for the historical facial itself. The movement arose partly from concern over skin damage from heavy stage makeup and lead-based cosmetics.

lead: Biganjutsu (the technique of the beautiful face) was an early Japanese method that framed facial skin care as basic hygiene. Wikipedia ties its emergence to two events: the 1887 Nakamura Incident, in which a kabuki actor reportedly suffered "skin suffocation" from heavy stage makeup, and a 1900 law banning lead-based makeup that raised awareness of lead poisoning [1].

The typical facial available in urban areas involved placing a hot towel on the face to open the pores, massaging with cream, and using electrotherapeutic devices, with the aim of smooth, blemish- and wrinkle-free skin and a healthy complexion with natural beauty rather than heavy makeup [1]. For people interested in skin quality, it is an early example of treating complexion care as routine upkeep.

Scholars cited in encyclopedia coverage describe it as a forerunner of Japan's later esute aesthetics industry, and the term broadened to include other beauty services. No clinical studies have evaluated the original regimen.

chain: Warm towel opens pores and cream massage cleanses
Regular facial upkeep supports clear, smooth skin
Natural-looking complexion with less heavy makeup
angle.text: The regimen aimed at healthy, clear skin through routine facial treatment. Its premise was that good skin lessens the need for heavy makeup.

infobox: Smooth, clear skin with natural beauty

paras: Concern over damage from stage makeup and lead-based cosmetics fed the idea of skin care as hygiene [1]. The Taisho period (1912-1926) saw growing Westernisation centred on Ginza, where Shiseido, which launched its Eudermine lotion in 1897, introduced seven skin-tone powders in 1923 in place of a single white shade, promoting natural skin colour [1]. The same source does not explicitly link these products to biganjutsu [1].
Treatment included a hot towel, cream massage and electrotherapeutic devices, aimed at a natural, healthy finish [1].
The article notes that in the Heisei period (1989-2019) natural, healthy, clear skin became the standard in Japan [1].

timeline.event: Nakamura Incident, a kabuki actor's reported skin harm from heavy makeup [1].
